summary: PCEP carries path computation requests and answers between clients and path computation elements. This document defines PCEPS, which uses TLS to provide a secure transport for PCEP so the exchanges are protected from eavesdropping and tampering.

plainLanguage.summary: It puts the messages between route planners into a locked envelope so no one else can read or change them on the way.

subtitle: How PCEP sessions switch on TLS with a new StartTLS message instead of a separate port.

tldr.problem: PCEP carries path computation requests and replies that can be critical to network operation, but RFC 5440 left protection of those exchanges open without recommending one mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: Both peers first exchange a new StartTLS message over the TCP connection, then run a TLS handshake with mutual certificate authentication before any other PCEP message, including Open, is sent.
tldr.outcome: PCEP sessions can be encrypted and authenticated on the existing PCEP port. The RFC updates RFC 5440 and has since been updated by RFC 9916.

today: RFC 8253 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5440, and it has itself been updated by RFC 9916. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs TLS
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) for routes, and lets PCEs talk to each other. These requests and replies can be critical for network operation and resource allocation, so appropriate security becomes a key element.

RFC 5440 analyses the threats but does not recommend one protection mechanism. RFC 6952 stresses confidentiality, especially when the two endpoints are not in the same Autonomous System, because intercepted messages could leak sensitive information about computed paths and resources.

This document picks Transport Layer Security (TLS) because it supports peer authentication, message encryption and integrity. It calls the result PCEPS. TLS acts only as a container for the transport, so PCEP's own flexibility and extensibility are unchanged. For PCE-to-PCE exchanges, the initiating PCE simply plays the PCC role.
sections.plainLanguage: Route planners share information that matters a lot. Putting it in a locked box while it travels keeps nosy people from reading or changing it.

sections.title: How a PCEPS Session Starts
sections.content:
A PCEPS session is built in four steps: a TCP connection is established, the peers exchange StartTLS messages, a TLS connection is negotiated, and then normal PCEP messages flow as defined in RFC 5440.

The RFC deliberately uses StartTLS on the usual connection rather than asking for another port number for PCEPS. It argues this makes more efficient use of scarce port numbers and allows simpler configuration. Implementations SHOULD follow the TLS best practices of RFC 7525.

This changes what RFC 5440 says about initialization: Open is no longer always the first message. In a TLS session, StartTLS comes first, and the speaker must not start the OpenWait timer after TCP setup. It starts a StartTLSWait timer instead. The PCC acts as the TLS client and the PCE acts as the TLS server.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the real conversation, each side says, 'Let's use the secret code.' Only when both have said it do they switch to the code and begin talking.

sections.title: The StartTLS Exchange
sections.content:
The StartTLS message contains only the PCEP common header, with the Message-Type field set to 13. The PCC asks for TLS by sending it, and the PCE agrees by answering with its own StartTLS. A PCE configured for TLS only may send StartTLS immediately after TCP setup. Otherwise it MUST wait to see whether the PCC's first message is Open or StartTLS. The collision resolution rules for Open messages in RFC 5440 apply to StartTLS as well.

If a speaker cannot or will not use TLS, it returns a PCErr message in the clear with Error-Type 25 (PCEP StartTLS failure). Error-value 3 means it will not talk without TLS. Error-value 4 means it would accept a session without TLS, and the other side MAY retry without TLS, which SHOULD be limited to one attempt.

A PCC that supports both modes MUST try StartTLS first, and MAY fall back to Open if it receives a PCErr. A StartTLSWait timer starts after TCP setup. If no StartTLS, PCErr or Open arrives before it expires, the speaker sends a PCErr with Error-value 5 and releases the connection. The RECOMMENDED value is 60 seconds, and it MUST NOT be less than the OpenWait timer.

An existing PCEP session cannot be upgraded to TLS. It has to be closed and set up again.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side holds up a card that says 'secret code, please.' If one side cannot do the secret code, it says so, and they may decide to talk plainly once, if both are okay with that.

sections.title: TLS Setup and Peer Identity
sections.content:
Once StartTLS has been exchanged, the peers negotiate TLS under these restrictions: TLS 1.2 or later is REQUIRED, certificate-based mutual authentication is REQUIRED, a ciphersuite providing integrity protection is REQUIRED and one providing confidentiality is RECOMMENDED. Compression is OPTIONAL. Implementations MUST support TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and SHOULD support the 256-bit AES variant with SHA384.

Peer authentication must be available in two models. In the first, X.509 certificates are checked with the usual PKIX trust model: a configurable list of trusted certification authorities, validation per RFC 5280, revocation checking (CRL or OCSP) as a SHOULD, and host checks per RFC 6125 against a configured DNS name or IP address. In the second, peers are trusted by the fingerprint of their DER-encoded certificate, and SHA-256 MUST be supported as the hash.

After TLS is up, the OpenWait timer starts and normal PCEP begins. A peer that cannot be properly identified must be disconnected before any PCEP exchange. If TLS negotiation or the identity check fails, both peers MUST close the connection immediately, and the initiator SHOULD retry using the exponential back-off of RFC 5440.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides show ID cards before talking. If an ID looks wrong, the door is shut right away and nothing is said.

sections.title: Working with Older PCEP Speakers
sections.content:
StartTLS is designed not to disturb implementations that do not know it. A PCC without PCEPS support sends Open first. A PCE that only supports PCEPS sends StartTLS, which the PCC treats as an error and answers with a PCErr (Error-Type 1, Error-value 1). In the other direction, a PCE without PCEPS treats a StartTLS as an invalid Open and answers the same way. A StartTLS arriving at any other time is an unknown message, and the receiver replies with Error-Type 2 (capability not supported).

For upgrades, the RFC says speakers SHOULD allow sessions with and without TLS during the transition, and a redundant PCE MAY take over while another is upgraded. Once everyone is upgraded, support for the unsecured version SHOULD be removed. Both peers must support this document for TLS to work.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new route planners can still meet. The new one asks for the secret code first, and if the old one does not understand, they fall back to talking the old way.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limits
sections.content:
TLS provides confidentiality and fine-grained, policy-based peer authentication, but cannot address everything. Attacks that forge the underlying TCP connection, especially on long-lived connections, may call for extra protection such as the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925), which is described as complementary to TLS.

The TLS handshake and ciphers cost more computing power than plain TCP, so a malicious client can more easily create high load and mount denial of service. Ciphersuites that give integrity but no encryption SHOULD NOT be used by default. With certificate fingerprints, any two certificates with the same hash count as the same peer, so the hash must be uncompromised.

Implementations that still accept non-TLS connections are open to downgrade attacks (RFC 7457): an attacker could strip the StartTLS messages or inject a PCErr suggesting a retry without TLS. For this reason peers SHOULD default to strict TLS, and an operator override to allow unsecured connections SHOULD trigger a warning.
sections.plainLanguage: The locked box is strong, but a sneaky person might trick both sides into skipping it, so the safest rule is to always insist on the box.

sections.title: Registrations and Operator Controls
sections.content:
IANA allocated Message-Type 13 in the PCEP Messages registry for StartTLS, and a new PCEP-ERROR Error-Type 25 (PCEP StartTLS failure) with values 1 to 5, listed in the table below.

For operators, implementations SHOULD let them configure the StartTLSWait timer and must support general TLS configuration plus at least one of the two trust models. Operators SHOULD be able to see whether a session is protected, which TLS version, authentication method and ciphersuite is in use, why a certificate failed verification, and to inspect the peer's certificate. Failures of StartTLS with peers known to support PCEPS SHOULD raise a warning, and implementations SHOULD log errors and keep failure statistics. The RFC also suggests that the PCEP MIB and YANG module could be extended with TLS information.

The RFC does not define discovery of PCEPS support. It mentions drafts that propose advertising it in IGP PCE discovery or in DNS, and says a PCC MAY use DANE to verify its peer when it uses DNS discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official number for the 'secret code please' message, and operators get dials to see whether the code is on and why it failed.
